items.title: Peggy Scott’s writing career on ‘The Gilded Age’ echoes a Black journalist who made her own rules
items.summary:
Peggy Scott (played by Denée Benton) has spent much of The Gilded Age figuring out what kind of writer she wants to be. As a Black woman in the early 1900s …the journey hasn’t been an easy one. When a white newspaper offers to publish her work, Peggy discovers that the editor wants her to use a pen name and change her Black protagonist to a white character. This prompts Peggy to write for a Black newspaper instead.

Now in Season 4 , that question has become even more important as her literary career takes off and she prepares to marry Dr. William Kirkland (played by Jordan Donica). Her ambitions have put her at odds with people who have their own ideas about what her future should look like.

This storyline might be fictional, but the world Peggy was navigating was very real 

Erica Armstrong Dunbar , the show’s historical consultant and co-executive producer, has explained that Peggy is a composite character inspired by several Black women of the era who were creating professional opportunities for themselves, including journalists Ida B. Wells and Gertrude Bustill Mossell, as well as novelist Julia C. Collins. 

Mossell is a particularly fascinating person to discover.

Gertrude Mossell’s writing ambitions also took her into the Black press 

Born in Philadelphia in 1855, Mossell came from a prominent Black family with a strong tradition of education and civic involvement. Though her mother died when she was very young, her father encouraged Mossell and her sister to read. By the time she was a teenager, she was already writing. Her commencement speech on “influence,”…
items.t: Peggy Scott’s writing career on ‘The Gilded Age’ echoes a Black journalist who made her own rules

items.title: Experts say this belief makes facing death more comforting than believing in an afterlife
items.summary:
Most people don’t like to think too much about dying . It’s dark, it’s morbid—and can lead to crippling anxiety.

But flipping the script on death by focusing on one simple belief may take the sting away and lead to better mental health while still living. A 2026 study published in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction narrowed down a specific belief that was more impactful than simply believing in an afterlife .

Researchers from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that study participants who focused on the concept of symbolic immortality—the belief that one will be remembered after death (i.e., leave a legacy) had better mental health and decreased levels of substance use and behavioral addictions.

Symbolic immortality, explained 

In the study, researchers defined symbolic immortality as “the belief that one would be remembered by others after death” and “the sense that one would continue to exist symbolically after death through group identification, a legacy, and through the memory of others.”

Study participants (Israelis aged 18-70) who believed in their own symbolic immortality reported decreased levels of the following:

Mental health problems (anxiety, depression, PTSD, emotion regulation problems, sleep disturbances) 

Problematic substance use (cannabis, alcohol, prescription drugs) 

Behavioral addictions (gambling, gaming, social media, internet use, pornography, sexual behaviors) 

The researchers told News-Medical & Life Sciences , “The feeling that our lives matter and will continue to matter to other people may be an important…
items.t: Experts say this belief makes facing death more comforting than believing in an afterlife

items.title: Scientists studied thousands of conversations and found the repeatable pattern behind ‘chemistry’
items.summary:
Chemistry doesn’t have to be romantic. You can have friendly chemistry and professional chemistry. Of course, romantic chemistry is always great, too. It’s often believed to be one of those things that two people either have or don’t. There’s no way to define it or force it. Sometimes, you just hit it off. Other times, not so much.

Social scientists, however, might disagree with that notion. A team at Dartmouth College has been hard at work analyzing thousands of conversations to define the indefinable: what makes for a good conversation? 

Analyzing thousands of conversations reveals conversational patterns 

Psychologists at Dartmouth College were not content with the idea that a good conversation is something that’s “difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.” So they set out to find a way to measure what makes a conversation enjoyable.

They’re not the first to study good conversations. Previous research has shown that people with high similarity in the words they use and the topics they talk about score higher on romantic interest, group cohesion, and other metrics. But the authors of this study astutely pointed out that most existing research treats these attributes as an overall average—for example, for how much of the conversation were the participants aligned?

Instead, they argue that similarity is a “dynamic signal.” Conversations have a give-and-take. There will be places where people agree, where they’re similar, and where they diverge. That was the data the team really wanted to dig into.

After studying thousands of conversations between random…
items.t: Scientists studied thousands of conversations and found the repeatable pattern behind ‘chemistry’

items.title: Goldie Hawn says this simple happiness habit helps keep her depression at bay
items.summary:
Actress Goldie Hawn , 80, is passionate about mental health and has been open about her own struggles with depression and anxiety for decades.

Hawn’s mental health challenges began in her 20s when she was new to fame. She sought help and has continued to encourage others to do so by openly sharing her story. In 2003, she founded MindUP , a preventive mental health program to support students, educators, and their families. 

In a recent interview on The Jennifer Hudson Show , Hawn shared an easy trick she often uses to boost her happiness.

Goldie Hawn’s happiness trick 

Hawn also shared her happiness trick in an exclusive interview with PEOPLE .

“I smile at everybody,” she told the publication. “I’m on the street and I have a smile on my face. And you do receive back because people actually return that.”

She went on to explain that acknowledging others and connecting with them is more than “an act of kindness—it’s a state of mind.”

One place where she looks to acknowledge people is the elevator in her apartment.

“You’re in an elevator: ‘How are you today?’ ‘Oh, I’m feeling pretty good.’ ‘Oh, that’s good. I’m happy to hear that,'” she told PEOPLE . “I do that when I’m in New York in my elevator in the apartment. And people are so sweet. And then when they get in the elevator again, ‘Oh, I got to see you again!'”

In another interview on Khloe Kardashian’s podcast, Khloe in Wonderland , Hawn added that making herself smile is an instant happiness booster.

“If you are sad, but you make yourself smile—I don’t know, sometimes I walk down the street, and I kind of have a…
items.t: Goldie Hawn says this simple happiness habit helps keep her depression at bay

items.title: A satellite image revealed a Roman villa beneath his family’s field and a Trojan War mystery
items.summary:
A casual afternoon walk during lockdown led Jim Irvine to an extraordinary discovery hiding beneath a field in Rutland, England. 

While walking through his family’s farmland in 2020, Irvine noticed unusual pieces of pottery, tile, and oyster shells scattered among the wheat. Intrigued, Irvine decided to investigate, pulling up satellite imagery of the property. 

There, he spotted a crop mark that appeared to outline a rectangular building. It was “as if someone had drawn on my computer screen with a piece of chalk!” he told Historic England .

An archaeological investigation eventually revealed that Irvine had spotted a Roman villa complex dating to the 3rd or 4th century. The site included multiple buildings, boundary ditches, and what appears to have been a bathhouse. 

Inside one of those buildings was something considerably more spectacular and unlike anything previously discovered in Britain: a mosaic measuring about 36 by 23 feet, showing scenes from the Trojan War . 

“This is certainly the most exciting Roman mosaic discovery in the U.K. in the last century,” said archaeologist John Thomas , deputy director of the University of Leicester Archaeological Services, in a 2021 university statement .

Roman villa in Rutland contained a massive Trojan War mosaic 

Researchers initially linked the scenes in what would become known as the Ketton mosaic to Homer’s Iliad . One panel showed the chariot duel between Achilles and Hector. The second depicted Achilles dragging the defeated Hector’s corpse. The third showed King Priam, Hector’s father, placing gold vessels on…
items.t: A satellite image revealed a Roman villa beneath his family’s field and a Trojan War mystery

items.title: From Cyndi Lauper to Michael Jackson, talented singer impersonates nearly ‘We Are the World’ artist
items.summary:
Plenty of talented people could cover the 1985 USA for Africa charity song “We Are the World.” Still, Justin J. Moore expertly impersonated not one, not two, but 19 of the 21 soloists from the original.

Justin J. Moore recreated 19 voices from ‘We Are the World ‘ 

We’re talking male and female voices, from Michael Jackson and Bruce Springsteen to Tina Turner and Diana Ross. In fact, the impersonation that got the most compliments was Moore’s rendition of Cyndi Lauper.

Produced by Quincy Jones and written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie, “ We Are the World ” brought together some of the biggest voices in American music at the time. Each soloist gets only a short featured passage, but those snippets are so distinctive that listeners can often identify the singer almost instantly. In other words, the song is practically a vocal-impression obstacle course.

Here’s the full lineup Moore covered:

Lionel Richie

Stevie Wonder

Paul Simon

Kenny Rogers

James Ingram

Tina Turner

Billy Joel

Michael Jackson

She’s also a master mimicker herself. As a child, she practiced by imitating characters from Broadway albums like My Fair Lady and West Side Story , shifting…

items.title: ‘Frozen’ animator launches an interactive ASL learning app and vows to keep it free forever
items.summary:
Josh Staub has had quite a career. The renowned Disney animator and visual effects artist has worked on some of the biggest hits of the modern era, including Wreck-It Ralph , Tangled , and the iconic Frozen , which is more of a phenomenon than just a film.

But despite the accolades, he was ready for a new challenge. A few years ago, he began developing a script for a new animated series , a project that would take him on an incredible and unexpected journey.

New project sparks a deep connection with the Deaf community 

Staub began developing an idea for an animated series that would tackle big themes of family, empathy, and the ways we communicate with one another. There was just one complication: the animated family at the core of the series would include characters who are deaf.

Staub knew that if he wanted to pursue this idea, called Small Talk , he couldn’t simply translate parts of his script into American Sign Language for the animation. As a hearing person, he needed to really learn much more about Deaf culture and the community behind it.

He began learning ASL from a Deaf teacher, which he says is the absolute best way to learn. Staub took to the lessons immediately, writing in a LinkedIn post , “I began learning about Deaf culture and fell in love with the Deaf community, forging deep friendships.”

The people he met as he forged friendships within the Deaf community became collaborators on the series, helping shape the animation, filmmaking, story, and art behind the show.

But as Staub got further along on his journey, he began using ASL learning apps to…
items.t: ‘Frozen’ animator launches an interactive ASL learning app and vows to keep it free forever

items.title: Finally, someone explains why everyone needs subtitles when watching TV
items.summary:
It seems everyone needs subtitles nowadays in order to “hear” the television. This is something that has become more common over the past decade, and it’s caused people to question whether their hearing is going bad or whether actors have gotten lazy with enunciation . A 2025 AP-NORC poll found about one-third of U.S. adults always or often watch with subtitles, and adults under 45 are especially likely to do so.

So if you’ve been wondering if it’s just you who needs subtitles in order to watch the latest marathon-worthy show, worry no more. Vox video producer Edward Vega interviewed dialogue editor Austin Olivia Kendrick to get to the bottom of why we can’t seem to make out what the actors are saying anymore. It turns out it’s technology’s fault, and to get to how we got here, Vega and Kendrick took us back in time.

Why modern mics actually made things worse 

They first explained that way back when movies were first moving from silent film to spoken dialogue, actors had to enunciate and project loudly while speaking directly into a large microphone. If they spoke and moved like actors do today , it would sound almost as if someone were giving a drive-by soliloquy while circling the block. You’d only hear every other sentence or two.

But with today’s technology, microphones are so small they can be strapped just about anywhere on an actor. This allows the actor to move about the set freely and speak at a normal volume without worrying that their words won’t be picked up.

“A lot of people will ask, ‘Why don’t you just turn the dialogue up?’ Like, ‘Just turn it up.’…
items.t: Finally, someone explains why everyone needs subtitles when watching TV

items.title: Under or over? There actually is a ‘right’ way to hang a toilet paper roll.
items.summary:
Humans have debated things large and small over the millennia, from democracy to breastfeeding in public to how often people ought to wash their sheets . But perhaps the most silly-yet-surprisingly heated household debate is the one in which we argue over which way to hang the toilet paper roll.

The “over or under” question has plagued marriages and casual acquaintances alike for over 100 years, with both sides convinced they have the soundest reasoning for putting their toilet paper loose end over or loose end under. Some people feel so strongly about right vs. wrong TP hanging that they will even flip the roll over when they go to the bathroom in the homes of strangers.

Contrary to popular belief, it’s not merely an inconsequential preference. According to health experts and the inventor of the modern toilet paper roll, there is actually a “correct” way to hang toilet paper.

What is the correct way to hang a roll of toilet paper? 

First, let’s be clear about what we’re even talking about here with a visual. In the image below, left is “over” and right is “under.”

Toilet paper rolls hanging. Photo credit: Elya/Wikimedia Commons 

So which one is the right way? According to health experts, “over” is the way to go.

“One key to maintaining a hygienic washroom is minimizing contact between people and surfaces,” Dr. Christian Moro, associate professor of health sciences and medicine at Bond University on Australia’s Gold Coast, told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation . “Depending on the type of roll holder, [hanging the toilet paper ‘over’] often lowers the chance…
items.t: Under or over? There actually is a ‘right’ way to hang a toilet paper roll.

items.title: American orders Olive Garden-style chicken parm in Italy and the waiter’s response is perfect
items.summary:
One of the great things about America is that we have a relatively young culture, so many of the foods that we eat were brought over from other countries . That makes America a great place to try out all the different types of food from around the world.

However, we also like to put our own stamp on staples from around the globe that give the American version its own unique flair. Some foods that we claim originated overseas were actually first made right here in the U.S. of A. For example, chimichangas, which can be found in many Mexican restaurants, most likely originated in the state of Arizona. Crab Rangoon, a popular “Chinese” dish, is believed to have been created in the San Francisco Bay area, and spaghetti and meatballs is largely an Italian-American creation.

The video that broke the internet 

TikTok creator Gabby Donahue posted a video that’s the perfect example of how some ethnic foods get remixed once they become popular in the States. In a video with over 7 million views, her father shows a waiter in Italy a photo of chicken parmesan from Olive Garden so he can order it at the restaurant. The waiter’s reaction is an excellent example of someone trying to be polite while he cannot believe what he is seeing.

“My Boston Irish father trying to order a Google image of the Olive Garden chicken parm in Italy ,” Donahue wrote in the text overlay.

When the father showed the picture to the waiter, he seemed a bit confused about the image. “Only in the States,” he said. “It doesn’t exist in Italy.” The father couldn’t believe what he was hearing: “It doesn’t exist…

items.title: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.summary:
This story has been co-published by  Reasons to be Cheerful  and the  Outrider Foundation . 

I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.”  

The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” 

He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.”  

Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth 
 Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by:   

never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy 

Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to…
items.t: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future

items.title: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

In the bag 
 A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. 

“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” 

Michaela says: 
 I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. 

Bird’s-eye view 

In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds.

items.t: What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives

items.title: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
items.summary:
This story was originally published by Open Campus . 

W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen.

The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them.

“I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River.

New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College 
 A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts.

A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River.

While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students…
items.t: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
